hints: Focus on the definition of a chiral centre, a tetrahedral carbon bonded to four completely different groups.
Start by crossing out carbons that can never be chiral, such as C=O, CH3, CH2 and any carbon joined to two identical O atoms or two ring paths that are the same.
Work around each ring junction and each carbon bearing a CH3 group and check its four bonds, then count how many pass the four-different-groups test.
walkthrough:
**Recall what counts as chiral**

A chiral centre is an sp3 carbon with four single bonds to four different atoms or groups.

Rule to apply:
$$\text{chiral C = C bonded to 4 different groups, usually with H}$$

**Remove the obvious non-chiral carbons**

The carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ is planar so it cannot be chiral. Any $\text{CH}_3$ carbon and any $\text{CH}_2$ carbon cannot be chiral because they have repeated H atoms.

Also ignore any quaternary carbon joined to two O atoms in the peroxide bridge, as two of its bonds go to very similar O environments and it lacks H.

**Test the remaining sp3 ring carbons**

Look at the three carbons bearing $\text{CH}_3$ groups. Each has $\text{CH}_3$, H, and two different ring directions, so all three are chiral.

Then look at the fused ring junctions and the O-CH groups. Four more sp3 carbons each carry one H plus three different C or O containing fragments, so they are also chiral.

**Count and conclude**

Adding them together gives 3 methyl-bearing carbons + 4 other ring junction and ether carbons = 7 chiral centres in total.

$$3 + 4 = 7$$

options.A: 4 is too low. It usually comes from counting only the three CH3-bearing carbons plus one ring junction and missing the other fused-ring and C-O chiral carbons hidden in the complex cage structure.
options.B: 6 is one short. Students often miss one of the bridgehead or lactone ring junction carbons because the fused rings make the four different groups hard to see.
options.C: 7 is correct. After eliminating C=O, CH3, CH2 and the non-stereogenic acetal type carbon, seven sp3 carbons remain, each with H and three different carbon chain and oxygen fragments, so each is a chiral centre.
options.D: 8 is one too many. It comes from incorrectly counting the quaternary peroxide bridge carbon or the acetal carbon bonded to two O atoms as chiral, when its groups are not four different groups.
